questions.q: What does it mean to "parse" JSON?
options: Deleting unnecessary whitespace from a JSON file
Converting JSON text (a string of characters) into a real object/array your code can actually use
Encrypting a JSON payload before sending it
Compressing JSON into a binary format
questions.explain: Parsing turns raw JSON text into native data structures (like a Python dict) so your code can access fields directly.

questions.q: In Python, what does json.loads(raw_text) do?
options: Converts a native Python object into JSON text
Parses JSON text into a native Python object (e.g. a dict)
Loads a JSON file from disk only, never from a string
Validates JSON against a schema
questions.explain: json.loads ("load string") parses a JSON string into native Python objects; json.dumps does the reverse.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say it's a 'feature, not an inconvenience' that malformed JSON raises an exception when parsed?
options: Because exceptions make code run faster
Because silently continuing with broken/incomplete data is worse than failing immediately where the problem is visible
Because Python requires all errors to be exceptions
Because JSON parsing never actually fails in practice
questions.explain: Failing loudly surfaces the problem immediately, rather than letting broken or partial data silently propagate through the rest of the program.

questions.q: Why should you check a response's status code BEFORE calling .json() on it?
options: Status codes have no relationship to whether the body is valid JSON
A 500 or 404 response's body often isn't even JSON (e.g. an HTML error page), so parsing it first produces a confusing error that hides the real problem
Calling .json() always fails regardless of status code
It's purely a style preference with no practical effect
questions.explain: Checking status first lets you handle an error response correctly instead of getting a misleading parse failure when the body isn't JSON at all.

questions.q: Why does successfully parsing a JSON string NOT guarantee the data is safe to use?
options: Because parsing always fails
Because successful parsing only confirms valid JSON syntax — it says nothing about whether the expected fields and values are actually present
Because JSON can't represent objects
Because parsed JSON is always missing the "name" field
questions.explain: Valid syntax and correct shape are two different things — Lesson 8's schema concepts (required fields, allowed values) must still be checked after parsing succeeds.
